transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because things have been getting a bit... tangled up lately. At work, mostly. I'm a jeweler, you see, I do a lot of custom work and repairs, and it's always been a very precise kind of job. You have to be precise with the stones, with the metal, with the customers. But lately, when someone comes into the shop—say, Mrs. Gable, she brought in this lovely little vintage sapphire piece last Tuesday, or maybe it was Wednesday—and they ask me a simple question, like, "When will my ring repair be ready?" I try to answer them, I really do. But instead of just saying "next Friday," my mind sort of... slips the gears. I'll start talking about the repair, and then somehow I'm talking about the invoices I need to file, and from the invoices I start thinking about the garden soil I need to buy because the receipt for the soil was next to the invoice, and before I know it, I'm explaining my mortgage papers to them because the bank called while I was gardening. And I can see it in their faces, doctor. I can see them just completely losing the thread of what I'm saying, looking at me like I'm speaking a different language. It's so frustrating because I know what I want to say, but all these other thoughts just crowd in and spill out all over the counter, so to speak.
Are these difficulties with staying on topic and following conversations affecting your relationships with your customers or impacting your work performance?

Oh, yes, it really is. It’s... it's taking a terrible toll, honestly, and it breaks my heart because I've built this business from the ground up. I’ve actually had to cut way back on my custom work, which used to be my absolute favorite part of the job. There's nothing quite like sitting down with someone and sketching out a completely unique design, you know? But lately, during those client consultations, I just... I completely lose track of what we're doing. A bride will be talking about the specific bezel setting she wants for her grandmother's diamond, and I'll try to explain the process, but then I'm rambling about the history of platinum alloys, and by the end of the hour, I haven't even taken down her ring size or given her a quote. 

And because everything gets so jumbled up in my head, I'm missing my repair deadlines left and right. I used to be so incredibly punctual. If I told a customer their chain would be soldered by Tuesday, it was polished and in a little velvet pouch by Monday afternoon. Now, the days just sort of bleed together, and suddenly it's Thursday and the necklace is still sitting in the safe, untouched, and the customer is standing right there in the shop looking at me. It makes me look so unprofessional. 

Even the paperwork... well, the paperwork is a whole other disaster. I used to handle all the invoices myself. I prided myself on keeping the books immaculate, making sure every supplier was paid for every ounce of silver wire or polishing compound. But now, I'll look at an invoice and the numbers and line items just sort of swirl into other thoughts. I've had to ask my husband to start double-checking all of them for me. He has to come into the shop after he finishes his own workday, bless him, and he sits at the little desk in the back room just to make sure I haven't overpaid a vendor or completely forgotten to bill a customer for a sizing job. I never used to need help like that. I've been doing this for decades, and now I can't even get through a basic invoice without him having to fix my mistakes.
Do you find yourself forgetting things that you would normally remember, such as appointments or tasks?

Well, no, actually, it's not my memory at all. That’s the strange part, you see. I actually have a wonderful memory, I always have. If I have an appointment, say, a dentist appointment on a Thursday at 2:15, I know it's at 2:15. I don't need a reminder call or anything like that. And with the shop, I know exactly what needs to be done. I remember that the clasp on Mrs. Peterson's pearl necklace needs to be replaced with a 14-karat gold lobster clasp, not a spring ring, because spring rings catch on her scarves—she wears those lovely silk scarves, you know the ones, hand-painted, usually from Italy, she told me her daughter brings them back for her every summer. 

So the task itself, the memory of it, is perfectly intact in my brain. I don't forget that the necklace is sitting there in the safe. It's just that when I go to actually sit at the jeweler's bench and do the task, or when I try to explain the repair to her, that's when all those other thoughts just rush in and take over. I haven't forgotten to order the polishing compound or the silver flux, I just... I get lost in my own head on the way to doing it, if that makes sense. 

But the actual remembering? No, I don't have any trouble with that. My memory is sharp as a tack, honestly. I can still tell you the exact inventory numbers for the sterling silver box chains we carried back in 1998, which is completely useless information now, of course, since that supplier went out of business years ago, but it's still right there in my head. So, no, I really wouldn't say I'm forgetting things. It's more of a traffic jam of thoughts rather than a blank space, if you know what I mean.
Do you feel like your difficulties with staying on topic and following conversations are affecting your personal relationships outside of work?

Well, I haven't really noticed it causing a problem at home, honestly. My husband, bless him, he's just... he's so patient. We've been married for twenty-eight years this coming October—we got married right in the middle of autumn because I always loved the colors of the leaves changing, you know, those deep russet reds and the bright golds. It always reminded me of the different shades of citrine and garnet when you hold them up to the light. Anyway, he knows me so well by now. When we're sitting at the dinner table, and I start talking about a new supplier for rhodium plating, and then somehow end up talking about the neighbor's dog digging up my hydrangeas, and then suddenly I'm wondering out loud if we need to get the chimney swept before winter... he just sits there and nods. He doesn't look at me like I'm crazy or like I've lost my mind, the way the customers do. He just sort of lets me talk until I tire myself out, or he'll gently steer me back by asking if I want more potatoes. 

And as for my friends... well, I don't really see them as much lately anyway. I'm usually so exhausted by the time I get home from the shop, just from trying to keep my thoughts straight all day, that I don't have the energy to go out for coffee or to my book club. I used to love my book club. We were reading historical fiction mostly, though last year we did a whole series on biographies of famous women, which was fascinating. But now, I just prefer to stay home. So, I wouldn't say the talking issue is ruining my friendships or my marriage, no. It's really just the shop where it's causing such a disaster. At home, it's just... well, it's just me being me, and my husband is used to that, thank goodness. I don't know what I'd do without him, especially with how tangled up everything else feels right now.
Do you feel any physical sensations, like anxiety or tension, when you notice your thoughts getting jumbled and you're having trouble staying on topic?

Well, yes, I do get this... this awful physical feeling when the thoughts start piling up like that. It's like a buzzing, and I actually... I start doing this thing with my hands. When I get anxious about losing my train of thought and looking foolish in front of a customer, I'll rub my fingers together. And I don't just mean a little nervous fidget, I mean I will rub them together so hard and for so long that they actually get completely raw and sore. As a jeweler, your fingertips are everything, you know? You absolutely need that tactile sensitivity to feel if a bezel is perfectly smooth or if a tiny prong is catching on a polishing cloth, but I just rub and rub my fingers together like I'm trying to buff a deep scratch out of a piece of brass. I don't even realize I'm doing it until it hurts.

And the strangest part is, while I have all that nervous, tense energy making me wear out my own skin, the rest of me feels... heavy. My husband actually pointed it out just the other evening. He was sitting in the back room while I was trying to finish up a ring sizing, and he says I move so much slower at the bench now. He told me it looked like I was moving underwater. Even just reaching out and picking up my tweezers—the fine-point titanium ones I use for placing little melee diamonds, the ones with the really delicate tips—it just feels like it takes so much physical effort. It's like my arms weigh a hundred pounds each. 

So I've got this frantic, anxious rubbing going on with my fingers, but actually trying to do a deliberate physical task at the bench? It's just incredibly slow and exhausting. I used to fly through those repairs, my hands just dancing over the bench pin, but now every little movement feels like such a chore. It’s so frustrating because my mind is racing with all these jumbled thoughts, but my body is just dragging.
Do you ever worry that people might think you're losing your mind or that there's something seriously wrong with you when you have trouble staying on topic or explaining things?

Well, I don't... I wouldn't say I worry that they think I'm losing my mind, exactly. Not in those words. I mean, it's more that I worry they think I'm just terribly unprofessional or maybe that I don't care about their pieces. And that's what really breaks my heart, because I care so much. When someone brings in their grandmother's engagement ring, or a locket that's been in the family for four generations, they are trusting me with their history, you know? It's not just metal and stones, it's memories. Like this one lady, Mrs. Higgins, she brought in a cameo brooch last month—beautiful carved shell, probably late Victorian, with this delicate seed pearl halo—and she wanted it converted into a pendant because she doesn't wear brooches. 

And I knew exactly how to do it, I could see the whole process in my head, how I'd solder a hidden bail onto the back without damaging the shell, which is so tricky because heat can just ruin those old cameos in a second if you aren't careful. But when I tried to explain the process to her, to reassure her that her heirloom was safe with me, my thoughts just started tumbling over each other. I started talking about the melting point of silver solder, and then somehow I was talking about the different types of torches, and then I think I mentioned something about the price of propane going up... and I could see her face just sort of freeze. She looked at me like I was a completely different person than the jeweler she'd been coming to for ten years. 

She didn't say anything mean, she just sort of gathered up her purse and said she needed to think about it, and she took the cameo and left. And I just stood there, feeling so foolish. I didn't think she thought I was crazy, but I knew she thought I wasn't capable anymore. And that's... that's almost worse, isn't it? To have people look at you and decide they can't trust you to do the one thing you've dedicated your whole life to doing. So, no, I don't sit around worrying that people think I belong in an asylum or anything dramatic like that. But I do see the confusion in their eyes, and the hesitation, and it just makes me want to sink right through the floorboards. It's just so embarrassing to not be able to articulate what I know is right there in my head.
Do you often feel guilty or ashamed after you've had trouble explaining something to a customer or keeping your thoughts organized?

Oh, the guilt... it’s just awful. It doesn't just stop when the customer leaves the shop, you know. I take it all home with me. I'll go home and I just replay it all in my head, over and over again. Every single awkward conversation, like the one with Mrs. Higgins, or when I stammered through explaining a simple prong retipping to Mr. Abernathy last week... I just lie awake in bed, staring at the ceiling—we have that textured popcorn ceiling, the kind they put in during the late seventies, and I keep meaning to have it scraped but who has the time or the money right now—and I just replay every stutter, every confused look, and every single repair that I’ve had to delay because I’m moving so slowly at the bench. 

I just replay all of it like it's this undeniable proof that I’m a burden. And that's when the guilt really, really sets in, because I think about the shop and the financial side of things. A few years ago, we took out a second mortgage on the house to expand the storefront. We wanted to put in these beautiful new cherry wood display cases with built-in LED lighting, because the old halogen lights were just so hot and they made all the white gold and platinum look a bit yellow, which you absolutely don't want. It was a big risk, but we thought it was an investment. 

But now... now I keep thinking I’ve completely ruined our future by taking on that mortgage. If I can't even talk to the customers without scaring them off, and if I can't finish the repairs on time because my hands feel like lead, how on earth are we going to pay for it? My husband is so patient, like I told you, he really is a saint. He works so hard at his own job—he's in logistics, coordinating freight shipments, which is stressful enough with all the supply chain issues they've been having lately—and then he comes home to me, just sitting there uselessly, rubbing my fingers raw and crying over a late ring sizing. It's just suffocating. Every time I mess up a conversation or fall behind on a piece, it just feels like more proof that I'm dragging him down, and that I've doomed us both with that mortgage all because I wanted a prettier shop that I can't even run properly anymore.
Do you feel a significant difference in your mood when you're not at work or dealing with customers?

I wish I could say yes. I really wish I could tell you that as soon as I lock the front door of the shop and turn the 'Closed' sign around, all of this just lifts off me. But... no, it doesn't work like that at all. Honestly, it starts before I even leave the house. Most mornings I wake up with this... this flat, heavy sadness. It's like the color has completely drained out of the house before I even get to the shop. 

I'll just be sitting there at the kitchen island—we put in this lovely absolute black granite a few years ago, and it's usually so beautiful when the morning sun hits the little flecks of mica in the stone—but lately, I just sit there with my coffee, and everything just feels so gray and lifeless. It doesn't matter if I have a completely free Sunday with no customers to worry about, or if I'm just sitting in my own living room in my slippers. That heavy, flat feeling is just... it's already there the second I open my eyes. 

I used to love my mornings, you know? Waking up early, listening to the birds, maybe sketching out a new custom pendant design while the house was quiet and my husband was still asleep. I had this special sketchbook just for my morning ideas. But now, I just stare at the countertop and feel this awful weight. It doesn't matter where I am or who I'm talking to, the sadness is just sitting right there on my chest. So, getting away from work doesn't really change it at all. The environment changes, sure, but that gray feeling just follows me everywhere I go.
Do you notice any difference in how your thoughts are organized or how you behave when you're by yourself compared to when you're with other people?

Well, I suppose the thoughts are just as jumbled when I'm by myself, honestly. I’ll be sitting completely alone at my workbench—it’s this beautiful old maple jeweler's bench that I bought second-hand when I first started out, it has all these wonderful little shallow drawers for my burs and my needle files—and my mind will still be racing, or sometimes it just goes completely blank. But as for how I actually behave... I didn't even realize how much had changed until my husband pointed it out to me. 

You see, when I'm alone, I think I'm just working normally, maybe just feeling a bit tired. But he comes into the shop sometimes to bring me lunch, usually just a turkey sandwich from the little deli next door because he knows I forget to eat, and he says I'm just... I'm physically different. He says I move so much slower at the bench now. It's like I'm moving underwater. He was watching me try to prep a setting for a small sapphire the other day, and he told me later that it looked like even picking up my tweezers was taking this monumental effort. And these are my favorite tweezers! They're fine-tipped titanium, they weigh absolutely nothing, they're specifically designed to be an extension of your hand so you don't get hand fatigue when you're sorting tiny melee diamonds for pave work. But he's right, lately they feel like they weigh ten pounds. My arms just feel like lead when I'm sitting there by myself.

But then, on the flip side, when I'm around people or when I get really overwhelmed and anxious about a customer interaction, I do this entirely different thing. I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until it physically hurts, but I'll just sit there and rub my fingers together. I'll rub the pads of my thumbs against my index and middle fingers, just over and over and over again, almost frantically, until the skin is completely raw and sore. Which is terrible, because as a jeweler, your hands are your entire livelihood. You need your calluses to handle the hot metal, but you also need absolute sensitivity to feel the tension when you're pushing a prong over a delicate stone. But I just rub them and rub them until they ache. So I guess... whether I'm alone and moving like molasses, or feeling anxious and rubbing my hands raw, my body just isn't acting the way it's supposed to anymore.
Do you ever see or hear things that aren't really there?

Well... I suppose... yes. It’s strange, I haven't really wanted to admit this to anyone, not even my husband, because he already has enough on his plate with the freight logistics and all, but... yes. Sometimes, especially when the shop is completely quiet, like in the late afternoons when the foot traffic just completely dies down on our street... I'll be sitting out front at my bench, and I'll hear a woman's voice. Just a low mutter, but she's definitely saying my name. And it always sounds like it's coming from the polishing room in the back. 

We have the polishing room separated by this heavy fireproof door because of the dust collection system—you know, polishing compounds like rouge and Tripoli create this incredibly fine particulate dust, and you absolutely have to have a good ventilation hood or you'll be breathing it in all day, which is just terrible for your lungs over the years. So it's a separate room entirely. But I'll hear this woman muttering my name from back there, clear as day. 

And then... there's also a smell. Sometimes I'll just be sitting there, trying to focus on a piece, and suddenly I get this incredibly strong whiff of burning metal. Now, as a jeweler, you know exactly what that smells like. It's usually the smell of the flux burning off when you're soldering, or if you accidentally get the torch too close to a piece of steel binding wire and it sparks. It has this very distinct, sharp, acrid smell that catches right in the back of your throat. But the thing is, I'll smell it when my torches are completely off. The main oxygen and propane tanks will be entirely valved off at the wall—I'm always so paranoid about gas leaks, so I make absolutely sure to bleed the lines and shut the main valves the second I'm done soldering for the day—but I'll still smell that sharp, burning scent just filling the room. 

And it feels so incredibly real. Both the voice and the smell, they're so vivid that I actually get up from my bench, put down my tools, and walk all the way to the back of the shop to check. I'll push open the polishing room door expecting to see a customer who somehow wandered back there by mistake, or I'll go check all the torch connections again, just sniffing the air around the hoses. But there's never anyone there, and the tanks are always cold and shut tight. I just end up standing there in the empty shop, looking for someone who isn't there and a fire that doesn't exist. It's just so unnerving.
Do you hear the woman's voice or smell the burning metal all the time, or does it come and go?

Well, it definitely comes and goes. It's not a constant thing every single minute of the day, but... you know, it's funny you ask about the timing, because it actually started a while ago, before all this heavy, gray sadness I was telling you about even started. 

There was this stretch—this was before the depression really settled in and made everything so impossible—where I was actually still doing quite a lot. I was still running my evening jewelry-making classes, which I usually love. We were doing an introductory wire-wrapping course, and I always use this dead-soft copper wire for beginners because it's just so much more forgiving than sterling silver when you're first learning to use your round-nose pliers. I had a full class of six ladies. And I was still keeping up with my gardening at home, too. I grow these wonderful heirloom tomatoes, Cherokee Purples mostly, and they require just constant tending and pruning of the suckers so they don't completely overtake the trellises. So I was busy, I was active, I wasn't feeling that terrible weight yet. 

But during that time, for several weeks, I kept hearing those noises. The muttering from the polishing room just kept happening, even when I was setting up the benches for my students. And... well, along with the noises, I was also getting terribly worried that customers were watching the business. I'd be setting out the tools, and I'd just get this overwhelming, prickling feeling that people were standing out on the sidewalk, staring through the front display window, just scrutinizing everything I was doing. We have these large, plate-glass windows in the front—which are absolutely perfect for natural light when you're trying to color-match stones, but they offer zero privacy. 

So for those few weeks, I was just constantly on edge. I'd hear the noises from the back, and then I'd catch myself constantly peeking out the front window because I was so sure people were out there watching the shop, judging how I was running things. It was exhausting. So, to answer your question, it's not just happening now... it was happening back then, too, for weeks, even before the sadness made it so hard to move.
Do you find yourself repeatedly performing the action of rubbing your fingers together in response to any specific thoughts or worries?

No, I wouldn't say it's tied to any one specific thought or... or a particular worry playing on a loop in my head, if that's what you mean. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh dear, did I leave the pickle pot plugged in?"—which is a terrible thing to do, by the way, because if the acid solution boils dry it creates this toxic fume and absolutely ruins the copper tongs. Or I'm not obsessing over whether I miscalculated the alloy ratios for a custom rose gold pour. It’s nothing concrete like that. 

It’s really more just... this overwhelming wave of general anxiety that washes over me, usually when there's just too much external pressure all at once. Like, if a customer comes in wanting to redesign an entire heirloom estate collection. That actually happens more often than you'd think. People inherit these gorgeous Art Deco platinum rings, but they want the European-cut diamonds pulled out and the platinum melted down into something modern, which always breaks my heart just a little bit because the hand-pierced filigree work from the 1920s is just nearly impossible to replicate today with modern wax casting methods. But anyway, when someone is standing there at the counter, expecting me to be bubbly and creative and attentive, and maybe the shop phone is ringing at the same time, and I'm just feeling that heavy, awful sadness I mentioned... I just start rubbing my fingers. 

It's completely unconscious. I'm not trying to fix a bad thought in my head by doing it, or trying to prevent something bad from happening. My body just sort of takes over and does it on its own because the general pressure of existing in that moment is just too much. I'll just rub and rub the pads of my fingers together while I'm nodding at the customer, and I truly don't even realize I'm doing it until the friction actually burns the top layer of skin off. So, no, no specific thoughts... just my body's way of short-circuiting when everything gets to be too much, I suppose.
Do you feel compelled to rub your fingers together in a specific pattern or for a specific amount of time?

Well, no, not at all. It’s not like I have to do it three times, or tap my thumb to my index finger and then my middle finger, or keep doing it for exactly five minutes or anything rigid like that. There are no rules to it, I suppose. It’s really just this continuous, restless motion. 

You know, when you work with your hands for decades like I have—and I have to tell you, jewelers have just terrible hands, we really do, we're always covered in little micro-cuts from the jeweler's saw blades, and we get these incredibly thick calluses on our fingertips from gripping the hand files and the pliers all day long. Especially the half-round needle files, if you slip while you're smoothing out the inside of a ring shank, it just chews right through your skin. So my fingertips are already quite rough and textured. 

And when I start rubbing them together when I'm overwhelmed, I'm just sort of... feeling that texture, I guess? It almost feels like I'm checking the gauge of a piece of sterling wire, or maybe rolling a loose stone, like a little sapphire or a garnet, between my fingers to check the facets. I just do it until the overwhelming moment passes, or until the customer finally finishes talking, or honestly until my skin literally starts to feel raw and sting. There's no counting involved, no specific pattern... it just goes on until the pressure in my chest finally decides to ease up just a little bit.
Are you having trouble sleeping at night?

Well, yes, my sleep has just been absolutely dreadful lately. It’s... it’s like my brain just refuses to shut off when it’s supposed to. I’ll get into bed, usually around ten-thirty or eleven, which has been my routine for years, but instead of drifting off, I just lie there. And I mean, I just lie there for hours. 

My mind will start racing, mostly going over all the shop receipts from the day, trying to remember if I logged the sales tax correctly for an out-of-state shipping order, or worrying about the spot price of silver going up again. But it’s not just the business stuff, it’s these odd, racing thoughts, too. Like, I’ll suddenly start thinking about whether the flux paste I use for soldering is drying out, or if I remembered to turn off the ultrasonic cleaner, even though I know I did. And before I know it, I’m just tossing and turning, staring at the ceiling, and it’s two or three in the morning. 

And then, even when I finally do manage to fall asleep, it’s so restless. I’ll wake up before dawn, way before my alarm is set to go off, and that’s it. I’m just awake. I’ll try to close my eyes and settle back down, but the heavy, gray sadness I told you about just sort of settles right back onto my chest, and the thoughts start all over again. Sometimes I’ll just get up and make tea, but even then, I’m so exhausted. I just can't seem to get a full, proper night's rest anymore. It’s completely draining, honestly.
Do you feel like you have to perform the action of rubbing your fingers together to prevent something bad from happening?

No, no, not at all. It's really not like that. I know some people have those sorts of... compulsions, I suppose you'd call them, where they feel like if they don't tap a doorknob four times, their house will catch on fire, or if they don't wash their hands in a very specific way, they'll catch some dreadful disease. But it's nothing like that for me. 

I don't have any sort of magical thinking attached to the finger rubbing. I'm not sitting there at the jeweler's bench thinking, "Oh, if I don't rub my fingers together right now, my torch is going to explode," or "If I don't do this, the casting flask is going to crack in the kiln and ruin a week's worth of wax carving." Which, by the way, is a completely rational fear, because if the burnout cycle isn't programmed exactly right, or if the investment plaster hasn't cured properly, the thermal shock will absolutely shatter the mold, and all that molten silver just spills out into the bottom of the centrifuge, and it is a nightmare to clean up. But I don't rub my fingers to prevent that from happening. 

It's really just... as I was saying before, it's just a physical reaction to feeling completely overwhelmed. It's not a protective measure. It's just... a release valve, maybe? When the sadness gets too heavy, or the anxiety of just being in the shop and dealing with people gets to be too much, my hands just start moving. I'm not trying to ward off any bad luck or prevent a disaster. Honestly, most of the time, I'm just trying to survive the next five minutes of a conversation without bursting into tears right there over the glass display cases. So, no, there's no conscious thought of preventing anything bad. It just happens.
Do you feel like you have no control over the action of rubbing your fingers together when it happens?

Well, yes and no, I suppose. It’s... it's not like my hands have a mind of their own, exactly. I mean, I *could* stop if I really focused on it, maybe? But when it’s happening, I’m usually so wound up and anxious that I don't even realize I'm doing it until my fingers actually start to get sore. It's like my body just takes over because my brain is so overwhelmed. 

But you know, it's funny you ask about my hands moving, because my husband—he helps me out in the shop on weekends, mostly just running the register and taking in repairs—he actually pointed out something else recently. He said I’ve been moving so much slower at the jeweler's bench lately. And he's right, honestly. It’s... it’s this heavy, dragging feeling. Even just reaching over to grab my soldering tweezers, or picking up a small piece of silver solder with the flux brush... it feels like my arms are made of lead. 

I used to fly through ring sizings, just zip, zip, zip—cut the shank, solder in the sizing stock, file, sand, polish, done in twenty minutes. Now, it feels like an absolute chore just to get the torch lit. It's like I have to consciously force my muscles to do the things they've done by muscle memory for thirty years. So it's this strange contradiction, really. On one hand, I'm moving like I'm underwater, just so sluggish and exhausted, but then on the other hand, when the anxiety spikes, I'm rubbing my fingers together so frantically that I practically wear the skin off. It's exhausting, it really is. I don't know why my body is doing this, bouncing between feeling completely drained and then having this nervous, restless energy that I just can't seem to turn off.
Do you feel like the act of rubbing your fingers together is something you must do, or is it more of a habit that you've developed over time?

Gosh, a habit or something I must do... I really don't know how to answer that, to be perfectly honest with you. I'm not sure it neatly fits into either of those boxes. 

When I think of a habit, I think of things I do at the bench without thinking, but that actually serve some sort of purpose, you know? Like, over the years, I've developed this habit of always tapping my tweezers on the edge of the soldering block before I pick up a piece of gold, just to make sure there's no stray flux or old solder stuck to the tips. That's a habit. I don't have to do it, but I've just done it for so long that it's second nature. Or how I always wipe down my bench pin with a leather chamois before I start filing, just to keep the silver dust from getting cross-contaminated. 

But the finger rubbing... it doesn't feel like that. It's not a habit I developed over time like tapping my tweezers. But at the same time, I wouldn't say it's something I absolutely feel I must do, either. It's not like this driving urge where my brain is screaming at me that I have to rub my fingers together right that very second. 

It is more like... well, I don't know. I really don't. It just sort of starts happening on its own. I'll just be sitting there, maybe trying to focus on setting a tiny little two-millimeter sapphire into a bezel, which takes an incredible amount of concentration, by the way, because if you push the bezel rocker even a fraction of a millimeter too hard, you can chip the stone. Sapphires are hard, sure, but they can still cleave if you hit them at the wrong angle with a steel tool. And while I'm trying to focus through all this heavy, awful sadness, I'll suddenly realize my other hand is just rubbing and rubbing in my lap. My fingers get so rough anyway from the needle files and the emery paper that I can practically hear the skin catching when I do it. 

So I don't know if that makes it a habit or a necessity or what. I've never really stopped to think about the exact definition of it. I wish I could give you a better answer, a simple one or the other, but I honestly just don't know how to label it. It's just something my hands do when everything else feels like too much.
Are there any areas of your personal life or relationships outside of work where you feel like your symptoms are having a significant impact?
